The historian's name was Rosalia Lo Bianco. She was a slight woman of sixty, with her glasses on the tip of her nose and an almost religious passion for dusty archives. Ever since she had read in the papers about the child hidden in the Caravaggio, she had spent every afternoon in the archive of Syracuse Cathedral, among seventeenth-century registers nobody had opened for three hundred years. Turi brought her coffee, just as he brought it to Matei on the scaffolding.

She had found the document on a Tuesday in December, at five in the afternoon, when the light was already fading. It was a single line, in a register of expenses, written in ink that had turned brown: "Paid three tarì to a boy called Salvatore, son of a washerwoman, for having served as a model for the foreign painter." The date was November 1608. The painter's name wasn't there.

The professor had phoned Turi immediately, from the archive corridor, in a whisper, as if someone might steal her discovery. Turi was locking up the church. He left the keys in the door, something that had never happened to him in fifty years, and ran across the square, at his age, his sacristan's coat flapping against his legs. When he arrived, out of breath, the professor put the register in front of him without a word.

Turi wrote the letter that same evening, in his shaky handwriting, on three sheets of lined paper. "Dear friends," it began, "I may be a silly old man, but I'm almost sure we've found our Totò. Totò is Salvatore, everyone in Sicily knows that. And in 1608 there was only one famous foreign painter in Syracuse. It can't be a coincidence."

At the workshop, the letter split everyone into two camps. On one side were Matei and Pietro, convinced one hundred per cent. "It must be him," Pietro kept saying. "I gave him the right name without knowing. I'm a genius." On the other was Bellini, who answered every burst of enthusiasm with a "maybe" or a "not necessarily". Giulia and Chiara were in the middle, changing their minds every two hours.

"It's possible it's him," Bellini said, "but it's also possible the foreign painter was someone else. In 1608 there could have been a Flemish painter passing through Syracuse, a Neapolitan, a painter of votive offerings. I doubt the registers would have called Caravaggio 'the foreign painter'. He was too famous, and too dangerous. They would have written his name." Matei shook his head. "Or maybe they didn't want to write it precisely because he was dangerous."

Bellini stopped. He looked at Matei for a long time, then said: "That, Popa, is the first intelligent thing I've heard in a week." It was true: Caravaggio had fled from Malta, where he had been imprisoned. In Syracuse he was a fugitive. It may be that whoever paid his models preferred not to write his name in the registers. But it was only a hypothesis. "A beautiful hypothesis," Bellini concluded. "And beautiful hypotheses are the most dangerous ones."

Davide, on the other hand, didn't take part in the discussions. He listened and drew. A week later he brought a sheet of paper to the workshop: a young woman kneeling by the sea, washing clothes on a stone, and next to her a child with curly hair looking at something outside the drawing, his eyes wide open. "Agata and Salvatore," he said. Bellini looked at it for a long time. "We don't know if they looked like this," he said. "But perhaps they did."

Christmas went by amid these discussions. The family, gathered in the trattoria, held a vote at dinner: eleven votes for "it's definitely him", three for "it's likely", one for "maybe" (Bellini) and one for "woof" (Lupino, who voted by raising his paw). Assunta, on the phone from Naples, said there was no need to vote: "In Sicily a child called Salvatore has been called Totò for four hundred years. What more do you want?"

Chiara, meanwhile, had done a little research of her own. A doubt had occurred to her: how much were three tarì worth in 1608? She had written to a professor in Bologna, an old friend of her grandmother's and an expert on old coins. The answer came after New Year: three tarì were roughly a week's bread for a poor family. "Not much," said Chiara. "But for a washerwoman, it was probably a small fortune."

On the twentieth of January a second letter arrived. This time it wasn't from Turi, but from Professor Lo Bianco herself, on University of Catania letterhead. Giulia opened it with trembling hands, in front of everyone, in the workshop. The historian had kept searching all through December. And in a second register, the expenses of the city Senate, she had found another line.

Giulia read aloud: "November 1608. Paid twenty scudi to Michelangelo Merisi, painter, for the painting of Saint Lucy. And three tarì to the washerwoman Agata, for her son Salvatore, who served the said painter." Nobody in the workshop spoke. Then Pietro let out a shout that made Lupino bark and Viola cry. "I told you so! It's him! It's definitely him!"

Viola, who was in Giulia's arms and had stopped crying, looked at all those grown-ups jumping about and hugging each other. Then she pointed at Davide's drawing on the wall, the one of Agata and the child, and clearly said her second word, after "guadda": "Totò!" The whole workshop burst out laughing. Pietro picked her up and spun her round. "See? She's sure too!"

Everyone turned to Bellini. The professor took the letter from Giulia's hands, put on his glasses and read it twice, slowly. Then he folded it and put it in the breast pocket of his jacket. "Now," he said, "it's very likely that it's him. Very, very likely." "But not certain?" asked Pietro, disappointed. Bellini smiled. "I'll only be certain when Totò wakes up and tells me himself."

That evening Matei phoned Turi. The old sacristan answered on the first ring, as if he had been waiting by the phone for days. He said almost nothing. He just listened, and at the end he said, his voice breaking: "Salvatore. Son of a washerwoman. He must have been six. I wonder if he knew he'd stay in that painting for ever." Then he added: "Tomorrow I'm changing the sign. I've earned it."

Concetta wanted to have her say too. The next morning she phoned Giulia at seven, before coffee. "I knew it," she said. "Agata was a washerwoman from Ortigia. The washerwomen washed at the Arethusa spring, a hundred metres from my house. That child grew up in front of my lemon trees, four hundred years ago." Giulia didn't have the heart to tell her it was only a hypothesis. In fact, now that she thought about it, it seemed a beautiful one.

The new sign next to the X-ray was handwritten by Turi, and the Heritage Authority, for once, didn't have the heart to replace it with a printed one. It said: "Totò. Probably Salvatore, son of the washerwoman Agata, Caravaggio's model in 1608. He may have been six. He definitely had wide-open eyes. Let him sleep."

In Florence, Pietro framed a copy of the professor's letter and hung it in his bedroom, above the bed, next to Lupino's contract. Underneath, in felt-tip pen, he wrote a single sentence which, in his view, summed up the whole story: "Maybe, probably, definitely: Totò." Bellini, when he saw it, said that from a scientific point of view it was an incorrect sentence. Then he asked Pietro to make him a copy.
